CALIFORNIA LIMITED OFFERING EXEMPTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jane Doe, states what California law provides about the limited offering exemption from securities qualification found at California Corporations Code § 25102(f) — a state-law exemption sometimes relied on for a narrowly offered sale of securities, such as to friends, family, or other insiders, by Acme Corp. Section 25102(f) exempts a qualifying offer or sale from the qualification (registration) requirement of Corporations Code § 25110; it is a distinct exemption, available independently of whether the same offering also relies on a federal Regulation D exemption. Where a specific business name is named below, that is Acme Corp.; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what this statute and its implementing regulation say. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular offer or sale by Acme Corp. meets the conditions of this exemption, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

THE 35-PURCHASER LIMIT AND THE RELATIONSHIP/SOPHISTICATION REQUIREMENT
California Corporations Code § 25102(f) exempts a qualifying offer or sale of a security from the qualification requirement of Section 25110 if the transaction meets each of several statutory criteria. Two of those criteria govern who may purchase. First, the security may not be sold to more than 35 persons in the transaction, counting persons both inside and outside California. Second, every purchaser must either have a preexisting personal or business relationship with the offeror (or with any of the offeror's partners, officers, directors, or controlling persons — or, if the offeror is a limited liability company, its managers) or, by reason of the purchaser's own business or financial experience (or that of the purchaser's unaffiliated, uncompensated professional adviser), be one who could reasonably be assumed capable of protecting the purchaser's own interests in the transaction. The statute itself excludes certain persons from the 35-purchaser count — including officers, directors, and affiliates of the issuer, and purchasers who qualify under a separate institutional-investor exemption in the same section (subdivision (i)) — and provides that spouses are counted as a single person, as is an organization not formed specifically for the purpose of making the purchase.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(f) Any offer or sale of any security in a transaction (other than an offer or sale to a pension or profit-sharing trust of the issuer) that meets each of the following criteria: (1) Sales of the security are not made to more than 35 persons, including persons not in this state. (2) All purchasers either have a preexisting personal or business relationship with the offeror or any of its partners, officers, directors or controlling persons, or managers (as appointed or elected by the members) if the offeror is a limited liability company, or by reason of their business or financial experience or the business or financial experience of their professional advisers who are unaffiliated with and who are not compensated by the issuer or any affiliate or selling agent of the issuer, directly or indirectly, could be reasonably assumed to have the capacity to protect their own interests in connection with the transaction."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(f), (f)(1)-(2), California Corporations Code, limited offering exemption — 35-purchaser limit and preexisting relationship/sophistication test (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25102.)
  Known gap: Corporations Code § 25102(f)(1) and (f)(2) are two paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision — Section 25102(f) — not independent sources of authority; this clause and the two authority clauses that follow it in this document all draw on different paragraphs of that same subdivision. The quoted citation below covers the subdivision's opening clause and paragraphs (1) and (2); it does not itself quote the statute's separate purchaser-counting exclusions (for officers, directors, affiliates, spouses, and certain entities not formed to make the purchase), which are summarized, but not quoted verbatim, in the body above. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular purchaser has a qualifying preexisting relationship or the requisite business or financial sophistication, and it does not address the many other, separately conditioned limited-offering and private-transaction exemptions found elsewhere in Section 25102 (including subdivisions (h), (i), (n), (p), (q), and (r)), each of which has its own distinct requirements not covered by this document.

INVESTMENT REPRESENTATION AND THE NO-ADVERTISEMENT CONDITION
Two further conditions of the Section 25102(f) exemption govern how the offer and sale must be conducted. Each purchaser must represent that the purchaser is buying for the purchaser's own account (or, if the purchaser is a trustee, for a trust account) and not with a view toward reselling or otherwise distributing the security. And the offer and sale, taken as a whole, must not be accomplished by the publication of any advertisement — a condition addressed independently in this California statute from the prohibition on general solicitation found in the federal Regulation D exemption discussed elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(3) Each purchaser represents that the purchaser is purchasing for the purchaser’s own account (or a trust account if the purchaser is a trustee) and not with a view to or for sale in connection with any distribution of the security. (4) The offer and sale of the security is not accomplished by the publication of any advertisement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(f)(3)-(4), California Corporations Code, limited offering exemption — investment-intent representation and prohibition on advertisement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25102.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Corporations Code § 25102(f)(3) and (f)(4) — two paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision, Section 25102(f), quoted in the preceding clause of this document; they are not independent sources. The statute does not define "advertisement" for purposes of paragraph (4), and this clause does not attempt to define it. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular purchaser's investment representation is accurate, whether any particular communication would constitute a prohibited advertisement, or whether use of a written offering or disclosure document, by itself, would violate paragraph (4).

THE STATUTE'S OWN NOTICE-FILING DIRECTIVE AND CURE PROVISION
Section 25102(f) itself directs the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation to require, by rule, that an issuer file a notice of a transaction conducted under this exemption; the statute does not itself state the filing deadline, leaving that to the Commissioner's implementing regulation (addressed in the next clause). The statute is explicit, however, that failing to file the notice, or filing it late, does not by itself forfeit the exemption. Instead, an issuer that fails to file the required notice must, within 15 business days after discovering the failure or after the Commissioner demands the notice — whichever happens first — file the notice and pay the Commissioner a fee equal to what would have been payable had the transaction instead been qualified (registered) under Section 25110.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "The commissioner shall by rule require the issuer to file a notice of transactions under this subdivision. The failure to file the notice or the failure to file the notice within the time specified by the rule of the commissioner shall not affect the availability of the exemption. Any issuer that fails to file the notice as provided by rule of the commissioner shall, within 15 business days after discovery of the failure to file the notice or after demand by the commissioner, whichever occurs first, file the notice and pay to the commissioner a fee equal to the fee payable had the transaction been qualified under Section 25110."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(f) (unlettered notice-filing and cure paragraph), California Corporations Code, limited offering exemption — statutory directive to require notice by rule, and cure/fee provision for a late or missed notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25102.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the unlettered paragraph of Corporations Code § 25102(f) that follows paragraph (f)(4) — the same statutory subdivision quoted in the two preceding clauses of this document, not an independent source. That paragraph is not itself separately lettered or numbered in the current, 2022-amended (effective January 1, 2023) text of Section 25102 fetched for this document. A separately verified regulation, 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.102.14 (in Item 2 of the instructions to its notice form), cross-references this cure provision as "Corporations Code section 25102(f)(4)" — a citation that does not match the current statutory paragraph lettering, since current paragraph (4) is the no-advertisement condition quoted in the preceding clause of this document, not the notice/cure paragraph. This appears to be an unrevised cross-reference carried forward in the regulation rather than an error in the statute's current text; this document does not further resolve that discrepancy, and a person relying on this document should not assume the regulation's internal cross-references to statutory paragraph numbers are current. This clause does not itself state what the filing deadline is — that is addressed, from the implementing regulation, in the next clause.

THE 15-CALENDAR-DAY DEADLINE AND FORM 25102(F) UNDER THE IMPLEMENTING REGULATION
The Commissioner's regulation implementing the notice-filing requirement described in the preceding clause is 10 California Code of Regulations § 260.102.14. It sets the deadline the statute itself leaves open: a notice under Section 25102(f) must be filed with the Commissioner no later than 15 calendar days after the first sale of a security in the transaction in California, and no notice at all is required if none of the securities in the transaction are purchased in California. The regulation also gives an issuer that is separately relying on the federal Regulation D exemption an optional shortcut: if the issuer is filing a notice with the SEC under Regulation D (or under former Securities Act § 4(6)), the California notice may simply be a copy of that federal filing, accompanied by the statutory fee and — for an issuer that is not a California corporation — a consent to service of process. The Commissioner's form for this notice is titled "Notice of Transaction Pursuant to Corporations Code Section 25102(f)," commonly referred to for short as "Form 25102(f)."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(a) An issuer who conducts a transaction under section 25102(f) of the Code shall file a notice with the Commissioner as follows: (1) If in connection with the transaction the issuer is filing a notice with the Securities and Exchange Commission pursuant to section 4(6) of the Securities Act of 1933 or Regulation D (Rule 230.503), the notice may be a copy of the form first filed pursuant to those provisions. The fee required by section 25608(c) of the Code must accompany the filing. Each issuer (other than a California corporation) must also file a consent to service of process (Form 260.165), unless it already has a consent to service on file with the Commissioner. The filing should be accompanied with a cover letter indicating that the filing is pursuant to section 25102(f), and if a consent to service is not included, a statement that the issuer already has a consent to service on file with the Commissioner. (2) Unless a notice is filed pursuant to paragraph (1), the notice shall be filed electronically through the Internet process made available by the Department at www.dbo.ca.gov. If the issuer claims the exception under subsection (f), the notice shall be in the form and contain the information specified by subsection (c) and in accordance with the instructions in subsection (d)."
  — 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.102.14(a), California Code of Regulations, notice-of-transaction filing mechanics for the Section 25102(f) exemption, including the Regulation D dual-filing option (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-260.102.14)
  "(b) A notice required by this section shall be filed with the Commissioner no later than 15 calendar days after the first sale of a security in the transaction in this state. No notice is required if none of the securities offered are purchased in this state."
  — 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.102.14(b), California Code of Regulations, 15-calendar-day filing deadline for the Section 25102(f) notice (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-260.102.14)
  "NOTICE OF TRANSACTION PURSUANT TO CORPORATIONS CODE SECTION 25102(f)"
  — 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.102.14(c) (form title), California Code of Regulations, title of the prescribed notice form (https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-260.102.14)

This regulation's text was verified through two independently fetched copies of the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute's mirror of the California Code of Regulations (using two different User-Agent strings), which were byte-for-byte identical to each other after whitespace normalization; the official state platform for the current Code of Regulations (govt.westlaw.com, used under contract with the Office of Administrative Law) could not be retrieved as a scripted fetch during this research — attempts returned a "Document not found" page and, for a search query, an unresolved redirect — so this citation was not independently cross-checked against that primary state-hosted source, unlike the Corporations Code citations in this document, which were verified directly against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov. This clause does not restate the regulation's electronic-filing default and its consequences, its narrow hardship exception for paper filing, or its filing-fee schedule.

HOW THE PURCHASER-BASED CONDITIONS DIFFER FROM REGULATION D
Section 25102(f) is a state-law-only exemption from qualification under Corporations Code § 25110; nothing in its text conditions its availability on the same offering also qualifying for a federal Regulation D exemption, and the exemption's own conditions are not defined by reference to the federal "accredited investor" concept that Regulation D uses. Concretely, the two frameworks' purchaser-based conditions differ: Section 25102(f) permits no more than 35 purchasers total, counting both California and out-of-state purchasers (subject to the statute's own exclusions for certain insiders and institutional purchasers), and requires every purchaser — regardless of wealth or income — to either have a preexisting relationship with the issuer or its principals or be sophisticated; Regulation D's Rule 506(b), by contrast, permits an unlimited number of accredited investors plus up to 35 non-accredited purchasers within any 90-calendar-day period, and tests only the non-accredited purchasers for sophistication. The one point at which the two frameworks are administratively linked, rather than substantively unified, is the dual-filing accommodation in the implementing regulation described in the preceding clause: an issuer relying on both exemptions for the same transaction may satisfy California's own notice-filing requirement by submitting a copy of its federal Regulation D filing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "(f) Any offer or sale of any security in a transaction (other than an offer or sale to a pension or profit-sharing trust of the issuer) that meets each of the following criteria: (1) Sales of the security are not made to more than 35 persons, including persons not in this state. (2) All purchasers either have a preexisting personal or business relationship with the offeror or any of its partners, officers, directors or controlling persons, or managers (as appointed or elected by the members) if the offeror is a limited liability company, or by reason of their business or financial experience or the business or financial experience of their professional advisers who are unaffiliated with and who are not compensated by the issuer or any affiliate or selling agent of the issuer, directly or indirectly, could be reasonably assumed to have the capacity to protect their own interests in connection with the transaction."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(f), (f)(1)-(2), California Corporations Code, limited offering exemption — 35-purchaser limit and preexisting relationship/sophistication test (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=25102.)
  "(2) Specific conditions — (i) Limitation on number of purchasers. There are no more than, or the issuer reasonably believes that there are no more than, 35 purchasers of securities from the issuer in offerings under this section in any 90-calendar-day period."
  — 17 C.F.R. § 230.506(b)(2)(i), Regulation D, Rule 506(b) limitation on number of purchasers (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/230.506)
  Known gap: This clause compares only the purchaser-count and purchaser-qualification conditions of the two exemptions; it does not compare, and does not purport to compare, every other difference between them — including Regulation D Rule 506(c)'s accredited-investor verification obligations, the general-solicitation rules under Rule 506(b) versus 506(c), or the federal preemption of state qualification (as distinct from notice-filing) authority that this corpus addresses elsewhere for offerings that rely on Rule 506 as a federally covered security; Section 25102(f) is not itself a federally covered exemption and is not addressed by that preemption. The federal citation below, 17 C.F.R. § 230.506(b)(2)(i), is an independent regulatory source with no textual cross-reference to Corporations Code § 25102(f); the comparison this clause draws between the two is this document's own analysis of both verified texts, not a comparison stated in either source. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular offering would qualify under either framework, and it does not address the several other California exemptions in Section 25102 (noted in the first authority clause of this document) that have their own, differently structured purchaser conditions.

SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
I, Jane Doe, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of California's limited offering exemption under Corporations Code § 25102(f) and its implementing regulation, 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.102.14, for informational reference only. This information sheet does not evaluate whether any offer or sale of a security by Acme Corp. meets the conditions of this exemption, whether any required notice was properly or timely filed, or whether any other exemption (federal or state) is available or was properly relied upon, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

Business name under consideration, if applicable: Acme Corp.

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

Signature of Jane Doe: ☐ _________________________

citations.quote: (2) Specific conditions — (i) Limitation on number of purchasers. There are no more than, or the issuer reasonably believes that there are no more than, 35 purchasers of securities from the issuer in offerings under this section in any 90-calendar-day period.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause compares only the purchaser-count and purchaser-qualification conditions of the two exemptions; it does not compare, and does not purport to compare, every other difference between them — including Regulation D Rule 506(c)'s accredited-investor verification obligations, the general-solicitation rules under Rule 506(b) versus 506(c), or the federal preemption of state qualification (as distinct from notice-filing) authority that this corpus addresses elsewhere for offerings that rely on Rule 506 as a federally covered security; Section 25102(f) is not itself a federally covered exemption and is not addressed by that preemption. The federal citation below, 17 C.F.R. § 230.506(b)(2)(i), is an independent regulatory source with no textual cross-reference to Corporations Code § 25102(f); the comparison this clause draws between the two is this document's own analysis of both verified texts, not a comparison stated in either source. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular offering would qualify under either framework, and it does not address the several other California exemptions in Section 25102 (noted in the first authority clause of this document) that have their own, differently structured purchaser conditions.
